title: UI/UX Design Basics for Marketers
subtitle: Design landing pages, flows and forms people can actually use — mobile-first, accessible, AI-assisted and tested with real users
description:
Marketers shape user experience every day: landing pages, sign-up forms, checkout flows, emails and the pages behind every ad. Small UX problems quietly waste budget — confusing navigation, slow mobile pages, forms that ask too much, buttons people cannot find. This course gives marketers, creators and small-agency teams a practical foundation in UI and UX design without needing to become full-time product designers.

You will learn usability heuristics, user research from the messages you already have, user flows and information architecture, UX writing, wireframing, components and states in Figma, and how to use AI design tools such as Figma Make and prompt-to-UI generators without shipping generic or inaccessible pages. You will design mobile-first landing pages with ethical persuasion, apply WCAG 2.2 in practice, test pages with five-second, first-click and usability tests, size A/B tests properly and build a continuous improvement habit. Every lesson includes a narrated lecture, a hands-on exercise and ready-to-use templates.
outcomes: Evaluate pages and flows with usability heuristics and severity-rated findings
Turn customer messages and interviews into insights and design decisions
Map flows, structure navigation and write clear microcopy for buttons, forms and errors
Wireframe, build components with states and prototype in Figma, using AI tools responsibly
Design mobile-first landing pages that are fast, trustworthy and free of dark patterns
Apply WCAG 2.2 AA to pages, forms and content and test with tools and assistive technology
Plan five-second, first-click, usability and properly sized A/B tests and act on results

modules.summary: Understand what UI and UX are, why they drive marketing results, and how to evaluate any interface with proven heuristics and user insight.

lessons.title: UI, UX and why marketers should care
lessons.body:
### Two terms, one experience

- **User experience (UX)** is the whole experience a person has when trying to achieve something with your product, site or service: whether they can find what they need, understand it, trust it and complete their task without frustration.
- **User interface (UI)** is the part they see and interact with: layouts, buttons, forms, typography, colors, icons, states and feedback.

UI is a big part of UX, but UX also includes content, speed, reliability, customer service, pricing clarity and even what happens after a purchase.

### Why this is a marketing problem

Marketing spends money to bring people to a page. UX determines what happens next.

- An ad can be brilliant, but if the landing page is slow, confusing or broken on mobile, the budget is wasted.
- A sign-up form that asks for too much information loses people who were ready to convert.
- Confusing pricing pages create support tickets and abandoned carts.
- Poor accessibility excludes customers and can create legal exposure.

Improving UX is often one of the most cost-effective ways to improve marketing results, because it increases the value of traffic you already pay for.

### The UX mindset: you are not the user

The most important principle in UX is simple: **you are not your user**. You know your product, your jargon and where everything is. Visitors do not. They arrive distracted, on a small screen, often from an ad or a social post, with a specific question in mind.

Three habits of the UX mindset:

1. **Start from the user's goal**, not the company's message. "What is this person trying to do right now?"
2. **Observe behavior, not opinions.** What people do on a page is more reliable than what they say they like.
3. **Iterate.** Treat pages as hypotheses; test, learn and improve.

### Where marketers touch UX

| Marketing asset | UX questions |
|---|---|
| Landing pages | Does the page match the ad's promise? Is the next step obvious? |
| Forms and sign-ups | Are we asking only what we need? Are errors clear? |
| Email and SMS | Is the call to action clear on mobile? Are links easy to tap? |
| Website navigation | Can people find pricing, contact and key information fast? |
| Checkout and booking | Are costs clear up front? Are there unnecessary steps? |
| Social profiles and link-in-bio pages | Is the path from post to action short and clear? |
| Chat and customer support | Can people get help when stuck? |

### A simple UX quality model

Many teams use a set of qualities to judge an experience. A practical version:

```
Useful      — Does it meet a real need?
Usable      — Can people complete tasks easily?
Findable    — Can people locate what they need?
Credible    — Do people trust it?
Accessible  — Can people with disabilities use it?
Desirable   — Does it look and feel appealing and on-brand?
Fast        — Does it load and respond quickly, especially on mobile?
```

If any one fails, the experience fails for someone.

### Worked example: a webinar sign-up

A creator runs ads for a free webinar. Clicks are healthy, but few people register.

UX review findings:

- The ad promises "Grow on LinkedIn in 30 days" but the landing page headline says "Welcome to my community" — weak message match.
- The registration form asks for name, email, phone, company, job title, country, and "How did you hear about us?".
- On mobile, the register button is below a long biography.
- The page loads slowly because of a large background video.

Fixes: headline repeats the ad promise; form reduced to name and email (optional phone for reminders with clear consent); register button repeated near the top on mobile; video replaced with a compressed image. The creator then measures registrations per visitor over the next campaign rather than assuming the fixes worked.

### Common mistakes

- Treating UX as "making it pretty".
- Designing from the company's perspective ("what we want to say") instead of the user's goal.
- Judging pages on desktop only, when most social traffic is mobile.
- Changing many things based on opinions without measuring.

### How UX shows up in your numbers

UX problems rarely announce themselves. They appear as symptoms in the metrics marketers already watch:

| Symptom in your dashboard | Possible UX cause | Where to look first |
|---|---|---|
| High click-through on ads, low conversion on the page | Weak message match, slow load, unclear next step | Landing page on a mid-range phone |
| Many form starts, few form submissions | Too many fields, confusing errors, broken validation | Form analytics, session recordings |
| Lots of "How much is it?" DMs | Pricing hard to find or unclear | Navigation labels, pricing section |
| Refunds or cancellations soon after purchase | Expectations set badly before purchase | Offer copy, checkout summary |
| Mobile conversion far below desktop | Tap targets, keyboards, in-app browser issues | Mobile QA in the social apps you advertise on |

The point is not to guess. It is to connect a number you already track to a specific experience you can inspect.

### Hands-on: a 20-minute UX quick scan

Use this on any landing page or link-in-bio page. You need a phone, a notes app, and ideally one person who has never seen the page.

1. **Open the ad or post that drives traffic**, then tap through to the page on your phone, inside the same app (for example, from Instagram or TikTok). This reproduces the real path, including the in-app browser.
2. **Time the first meaningful view.** Count roughly how long until the headline and main button are visible. Note it.
3. **Five-second check.** Show the page to your helper for five seconds, then ask: "What is this offering, and who is it for?" Write down their words exactly.
4. **Complete the main task** (sign up, book, buy) with a test email address. Note every moment of hesitation.
5. **Score the seven qualities** from 1 to 5 using the template below.
6. **Pick one fix** you can make this week and one metric that should move.

```text
UX QUICK SCAN — [page name]            Date: ______  Device: ______  App/browser: ______
Traffic source: ______________________  Promise in ad/post: _____________________________

Quality       Score (1-5)   Evidence (what I saw or heard)
Useful        ___           ______________________________________________
Usable        ___           ______________________________________________
Findable      ___           ______________________________________________
Credible      ___           ______________________________________________
Accessible    ___           ______________________________________________
Desirable     ___           ______________________________________________
Fast          ___           ______________________________________________

Five-second answer (exact words): ____________________________________________
Biggest problem: _____________________________________________________________
One change to test: __________________________________________________________
Metric that should move (and baseline): _______________________________________
```

### Using an AI assistant as a second reviewer

AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini can act as a fast "second pair of eyes" on page copy. They cannot see how real users behave, so treat their output as hypotheses, never as evidence. A useful prompt:

```text
You are a senior UX reviewer. Here is the ad copy and the landing-page text (pasted below).
1) Summarize in one sentence what a first-time visitor would think the page offers.
2) List any mismatch between the ad's promise and the page.
3) List the top five questions or worries a cautious buyer might still have.
4) Flag unclear labels or jargon.
Do not invent facts about the business. Mark every point as a hypothesis to test.

AD: <paste>
PAGE TEXT: <paste>
```

Paste only public page content, never customer data. Then check the AI's hypotheses against real users in the testing lessons later in this course.

### How to measure success

Pick one primary metric per page (for example, registrations per landing-page visitor) and record a baseline before changing anything. Add one guardrail metric that should not get worse, such as refund requests or lead quality. Compare like with like: the same traffic source, similar days of the week, and enough time to smooth out random swings.

### Summary

UX is the whole experience of achieving a goal; UI is the visible, interactive layer. Marketers influence UX constantly, and improving it multiplies the value of traffic. Adopt the UX mindset — you are not the user — and judge experiences on usefulness, usability, findability, credibility, accessibility, desirability and speed.

video.script: Every time you run an ad, send an email or post a link, you're sending people into an experience. What happens next is user experience, or UX. UX is the whole experience someone has when they try to get something done: finding information, understanding it, trusting it and completing a task without frustration. The user interface, or UI, is the part they see and touch — the layout, the buttons, the forms, the colors and the feedback when they tap something. UI is a big part of UX, but UX also includes speed, content, pricing clarity and what happens after someone converts. Why should marketers care? Because marketing buys attention, and UX decides whether that attention turns into results. A great ad pointing to a slow, confusing mobile page wastes money. A form that asks for ten fields loses people who were ready to sign up. The most important idea in UX is simple: you are not your user. You know your product and your jargon. Your visitors arrive distracted, on a phone, with one question in mind. So start from their goal, watch what people actually do rather than what they say, and treat every page as a hypothesis you can improve. Here's a quick check you can run on any page. Is it useful? Is it easy to use? Can people find what they need? Do they trust it? Can people with disabilities use it? Does it feel appealing and on-brand? And is it fast, especially on mobile? If any one of those fails, the experience fails for someone. In this course, you'll learn to spot these problems and fix them.

scenes.narration: Picture this. You spend five hundred dollars on an ad. People love it. They click. And then almost nobody signs up. The ad did its job. So what went wrong? Nine times out of ten, the answer is what happened after the click. That's user experience. In this lecture, you'll learn the difference between UI and UX, why UX is really a marketing problem, the mindset that separates good pages from expensive ones, and a twenty-minute quick scan you can run on any page today. By the end, you'll know exactly where to look when clicks don't turn into customers.

lessons.title: The 10 usability heuristics in practice
lessons.body:
### A shared checklist for good interfaces

In the 1990s, usability expert Jakob Nielsen published ten general principles for interaction design, known as **usability heuristics**. They remain one of the most widely used tools for evaluating interfaces quickly. A heuristic evaluation — reviewing a page against these principles — takes little time and reliably uncovers common problems.

### The ten heuristics with marketing examples

| # | Heuristic | What it means | Marketing example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Visibility of system status | Keep users informed about what's happening | "Sending…" then "Thanks! Check your inbox" after a form submit; progress steps in checkout |
| 2 | Match between system and the real world | Use users' language and familiar concepts | "Book a call" instead of "Initiate consultation workflow" |
| 3 | User control and freedom | Provide clear ways to undo, go back or exit | Easy-to-find close button on pop-ups; editable cart |
| 4 | Consistency and standards | Follow platform and internal conventions | Links look like links; the logo returns home; buttons look the same site-wide |
| 5 | Error prevention | Prevent problems before they occur | Date pickers instead of free text; confirming before deleting |
| 6 | Recognition rather than recall | Make options visible instead of relying on memory | Showing selected plan details at checkout; recently viewed items |
| 7 | Flexibility and efficiency of use | Support both novices and experts | Autofill, saved details, shortcuts for returning customers |
| 8 | Aesthetic and minimalist design | Remove information that competes with what matters | One primary call to action per section |
| 9 | Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors | Plain-language error messages with solutions | "That email looks incomplete — did you mean name@gmail.com?" |
| 10 | Help and documentation | Provide easy-to-find help when needed | FAQs near pricing; chat link during checkout |

### Running a quick heuristic evaluation

1. **Define the task** you're evaluating ("Register for the webinar on mobile").
2. **Walk through the task** as a new user would, ideally on the device your audience uses.
3. **Note each problem**, the heuristic it breaks, and where it happens.
4. **Rate severity** — for example 0 (not a problem) to 4 (blocks the task).
5. **Recommend a fix** for each.
6. **Ideally, have two or three people evaluate independently**, then combine findings; different people spot different problems.

```
Heuristic evaluation log
Task: ________________________   Device: ________
No Location        Problem                       Heuristic  Severity  Fix
1  Form            No confirmation after submit   H1         3        Add success message + email
2  Pricing         "SKU tiers" jargon             H2         2        Rename to "Plans"
3  Pop-up          Close button tiny, low contrast H3        3        Larger, clear close button
```

### Severity helps prioritize

Not every issue matters equally. Prioritize:

- **Frequency:** how many users hit it?
- **Impact:** how badly does it block them?
- **Persistence:** is it a one-time annoyance or a repeated one?

Fix high-severity, high-frequency issues first. A missing confirmation message on a paid-traffic form may matter more than a slightly inconsistent icon.

### Limitations

Heuristic evaluation is fast and cheap but it is expert judgment, not user evidence. It misses problems specific to your audience's knowledge, context or language, and it can produce false alarms. Combine it with usability testing and analytics (covered later in the course).

### Worked example: a small e-commerce store

Task: "Buy a phone case on mobile."

Findings:

- H1: After tapping "Add to cart", nothing visible changes — users tap again and add two cases.
- H2: Shipping is called "fulfillment fee".
- H4: Some buttons are rounded and green, others square and gray.
- H5: The phone model is typed as free text, leading to mistakes.
- H9: Card errors say "Transaction failed (code 51)".
- H10: No delivery information until the last step.

Fixes: a toast message and cart badge update; "Shipping" wording; one button style; a model dropdown; human-readable payment errors with next steps; delivery times shown on product pages.

### Common mistakes

- Evaluating on desktop when most customers use mobile.
- Listing problems without severity, so teams fix trivial issues first.
- Treating heuristics as rigid rules rather than guides.
- Skipping real user testing because "we already did a heuristic review".

### Hands-on: run a heuristic review with a shared sheet

Set up a simple spreadsheet (Google Sheets, Excel or Airtable all work) with these columns, then have two or three people fill it in independently before you merge results.

```text
ID | Task | Screen/URL | Problem (observed) | Heuristic (H1-H10) | Frequency (1-3) | Impact (1-3) | Persistence (1-3) | Severity | Fix | Owner | Status
```

Add a formula to turn the three ratings into a single severity score so the team sorts by evidence rather than volume:

```text
Severity (in column I, row 2):   =ROUND((F2*2 + G2*3 + H2)/6*4, 0)
```

This weights impact most heavily and maps the result onto the familiar 0–4 scale. Adjust the weights if your team prefers, but agree on them before the review, not after.

Step by step:

1. **Choose one task and one device.** For example, "Buy a gift card on an Android phone from a Facebook ad."
2. **Walk the task twice.** First as a newcomer, reading everything. Then quickly, as a returning customer.
3. **Log only what you observe.** "Tapped 'Add to cart'; nothing changed" is an observation. "The cart is bad" is not.
4. **Tag the heuristic.** If a problem breaks two heuristics, choose the most specific one.
5. **Merge and de-duplicate.** Combine the reviewers' sheets, keep the clearest wording, and note how many reviewers found each issue.
6. **Sort by severity and pick the top three fixes** for the next sprint or campaign.

### Using AI to speed up (not replace) the review

You can paste screenshots or page text into a multimodal AI assistant and ask it to suggest potential heuristic violations. It is useful for breadth — it may spot jargon or missing feedback messages you overlooked — but it hallucinates problems and misses context. Use it as an extra reviewer whose findings must be confirmed on a real device:

```text
Act as a usability reviewer using Nielsen's 10 heuristics. For the attached screenshots of the
task "<task>" on mobile, list potential issues as: screen, observation, heuristic, why it matters.
Only list issues visible in the screenshots. Say "uncertain" when you are guessing.
```

### How to measure success

Track the number of high-severity issues open over time, and connect the top fixes to a task metric: task completion rate in usability tests, form completion rate, or support contacts about the same problem. A heuristic review "worked" when the specific problems it found stop appearing in recordings, tickets and tests.

### Summary

Nielsen's ten heuristics give you a fast, structured way to review any page or flow. Define a task, walk through it on the right device, log problems with the heuristic, severity and fix, and prioritize by frequency and impact — then validate with real users.

scenes.narration: Have you ever tapped a button, seen nothing happen, and tapped it again? And then discovered you'd ordered two of something? That tiny moment of confusion has a name, and a fix. In the nineteen nineties, usability expert Jakob Nielsen published ten general principles for interface design, called usability heuristics. Three decades later, they're still one of the fastest ways to find problems on any page. In this lecture, you'll learn all ten with marketing examples, how to run a quick heuristic review, how to score severity, and where this method falls short.

• Ten principles from Jakob Nielsen

scenes.narration: Why should a marketer care about a checklist from the nineties? Because heuristic reviews are fast and cheap. One person with a phone can review a landing page in thirty minutes and find the problems that are quietly wasting ad spend. No recruitment, no special tools. Think of heuristics like a pilot's pre-flight checklist. The pilot knows how to fly. The checklist makes sure nothing obvious gets missed when everyone's in a hurry. Before a campaign launch, you're in a hurry too. And because the ten heuristics are shared vocabulary, they also end arguments. Instead of saying I don't like this pop-up, you can say this breaks user control and freedom, because the close button is hard to find. That turns taste into a reasoned, fixable problem.
scenes.onScreen:

• Finds problems wasting ad spend
• Like a pilot's pre-flight checklist

scenes.narration: Let's go through the first five. One, visibility of system status. Keep people informed, like showing sending, then thanks, check your inbox, after a form submit. Two, match between the system and the real world. Use your customers' words. Book a call, not initiate consultation workflow. Three, user control and freedom. Give people a clear way to undo, go back or close, like a close button on a pop-up that's actually findable. Four, consistency and standards. Links look like links, and buttons look the same across the site. Five, error prevention. Stop mistakes before they happen, with a date picker instead of free text.

scenes.narration: Now six to ten. Six, recognition rather than recall. Show options instead of making people remember them, like displaying the chosen plan at checkout. Seven, flexibility and efficiency. Help newcomers and regulars, with autofill and saved details. Eight, aesthetic and minimalist design. Remove anything that competes with what matters, often one primary call to action per section. Nine, help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors. Instead of error code fifty-one, say your card was declined, please try another card. And ten, help and documentation. Put answers where questions arise, like an FAQ right beside pricing.

scenes.narration: Here's how to run a review. First, define one task, like register for the webinar on mobile. Second, walk through it as a new user would, on the device your audience actually uses. Third, log every problem: where it happens, which heuristic it breaks, and a suggested fix. Fourth, rate severity. A common scale runs from zero, not a problem, to four, blocks the task. Think about frequency, how many people hit it, impact, how badly it hurts, and persistence, whether it keeps happening. Fifth, if you can, have two or three people review independently. Different people spot different problems.

That's heuristic one. Shipping is labeled fulfillment fee. That's heuristic two. Some buttons are green and rounded, others gray and square. Heuristic four. The phone model is typed as free text, causing wrong orders. Heuristic five. And card errors say transaction failed, code fifty-one. Heuristic nine. Each fix is small. A cart badge and a toast message. The word shipping. One button style. A model dropdown. A human error message.

It might notice jargon or a missing confirmation message. But it also invents problems and misses context, like how your customers actually talk. So treat it as an extra reviewer whose findings you confirm on a real device. And remember the biggest limitation of heuristic reviews in general. They're expert judgment, not user evidence. They miss problems specific to your audience, and they create some false alarms. Combine them with usability testing and analytics.

scenes.narration: Let's get more precise about severity, because that's what turns a list into a plan. Ask three questions about each problem. How many people hit it? That's frequency. How badly does it hurt them? That's impact. And does it keep happening, or is it a one-time annoyance? That's persistence. In the lesson sheet, a simple formula weights impact the most and maps the result onto a zero to four scale. The exact weights matter less than agreeing on them before the review. Then sort. A missing confirmation on a paid-traffic form will almost always beat a slightly inconsistent footer icon.

Evaluate specific tasks on the device your audience actually uses.
Log each problem with the heuristic, severity and a recommended fix.
Heuristic reviews complement — but don't replace — testing with real users.

lessons.title: Understanding users: goals, jobs and lightweight research
lessons.body:
### Design starts with people

Every UX decision rests on assumptions about users: who they are, what they want, what they already know, and what worries them. Better assumptions — grounded in evidence — lead to better pages. You don't need a research department; lightweight methods get you most of the way.

### Goals, tasks and context

For each key audience, capture:

- **Goal:** what they ultimately want ("Get more clients for my salon").
- **Task:** what they are trying to do on this page right now ("Compare booking software prices").
- **Context:** device, place, time pressure, language, connection quality.
- **Anxieties:** what might stop them ("Hidden fees?", "Is my data safe?", "Will this work in my country?").
- **Knowledge:** familiarity with the category and jargon.

### Jobs to be done

The **jobs-to-be-done** idea frames users' needs as progress they're trying to make: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]."

Example: "When I'm launching a new product, I want to get a professional landing page live in a day, so I can start taking pre-orders before my competitors."

Job statements help you prioritize content: this user needs speed, templates and payment setup, not a long history of the company.

### Proto-personas

Full research-based personas take time. **Proto-personas** are quick, assumption-based profiles created from what the team knows, then validated over time.

```
Proto-persona
Name/label:     "Busy salon owner" (avoid stereotypes; focus on behavior)
Context:        Runs a 3-chair salon in Lahore; manages bookings on WhatsApp
Goal:           Reduce no-shows and admin time
Tasks on site:  Understand features, check price in local currency, see if it works with WhatsApp
Anxieties:      Cost, learning curve, staff adoption
Channels:       Instagram, Facebook groups, word of mouth
Evidence:       3 sales calls, 20 support chats (update as research grows)
```

Mark which parts are assumptions and which are evidenced.

### Lightweight research methods

| Method | What it gives you | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Customer interviews (5–8) | Motivations, language, anxieties | Low–medium |
| Support tickets, chats, DMs, reviews | Real problems in customers' words | Low |
| Sales call notes | Objections and decision criteria | Low |
| On-site surveys (one question) | Why people visit, what's missing | Low |
| Analytics | What people do, where they drop | Low–medium |
| Search queries (site search and search engines) | What people look for | Low |
| Usability tests | Where people struggle | Medium |

### Interview tips

- Ask about **past behavior**, not hypothetical futures: "Tell me about the last time you booked a…" rather than "Would you use…?"
- Ask open questions and follow up with "Why?" and "Tell me more".
- Avoid leading questions ("Don't you think this is easy?").
- Record (with consent) or take detailed notes; note exact phrases people use.
- Respect privacy: collect only what you need, explain how notes are used, and follow data-protection rules in your market.

### Turning research into design decisions

Research is only useful if it changes something. After collecting insights:

1. Cluster notes into themes (affinity mapping).
2. Write insights as statements: "Salon owners worry staff won't adopt new tools."
3. Turn insights into design implications: "Show a 'staff app in 5 minutes' video and a testimonial from a salon manager."
4. Prioritize implications for the pages that matter most.

### Worked example: a coaching program page

Research: 6 interviews and 50 DM questions. Themes: price uncertainty, time commitment, "Is this for beginners?", payment options in local currency.

Design implications: a "Who this is for / not for" section; weekly time commitment stated clearly; price shown in multiple currencies where appropriate with clear installment terms; FAQ addressing beginner concerns in the exact language people used.

### Common mistakes

- Designing for "everyone".
- Personas based on demographics only, with no goals or anxieties.
- Asking people to predict future behavior.
- Doing research and then ignoring it.

### Research ethics and privacy

Treat research participants with respect. Explain why you are talking to them, how long it will take and how notes or recordings will be used, and get their consent before recording. Store notes securely, remove personal details you do not need, and delete recordings when the project ends. Pay or reward participants fairly for their time, and never use research sessions as a disguised sales pitch.

### Hands-on: synthesize real customer messages in one hour

You probably already own a research goldmine: DMs, support tickets, reviews, sales-call notes and chat logs. This exercise turns them into design decisions.

1. **Export 30–50 recent messages** from one or two sources (for example, Instagram DMs and support emails). Remove names, phone numbers, emails and order numbers first.
2. **Paste each message onto its own card** in a whiteboard tool (FigJam, Miro or plain sticky notes).
3. **Cluster silently for 15 minutes.** Move cards that feel related together. Don't name groups yet.
4. **Name each cluster with a user-voice label**, such as "I don't know if this works with WhatsApp."
5. **Write an insight and a design implication** for the three largest clusters, using the template below.

```text
INSIGHT CARD
Cluster name (user voice): _____________________________________
How many messages: ___ of ___      Sources: ___________________
Insight (what we now believe): _________________________________
Evidence (2 short quotes): _____________________________________
Design implication (what we'll change): ________________________
Where (page/section): __________________ Metric to watch: _______
Confidence: low / medium / high     Next research step: __________
```

### Using AI to speed up synthesis (carefully)

AI assistants can do a useful first-pass clustering of anonymized text. Keep a human in charge of the final themes, because models can over-generalize or invent patterns.

```text
Below are 40 anonymized customer messages, one per line.
1) Group them into 4-7 themes. For each theme give: a short name in the customer's own words,
   the count of messages, and 2 verbatim quotes (copy exactly; do not paraphrase).
2) List any messages that do not fit a theme.
3) Do not infer demographics or facts that are not in the text.
MESSAGES:
<paste>
```

Then check every quote against the source messages. If a quote does not exist verbatim, discard that theme and redo it by hand.

**Privacy check:** only paste anonymized data, and use a business account or tool approved by your organization. Many AI services have settings for whether your inputs are used for training; check them before you start, and follow the data-protection rules that apply to your customers (for example, GDPR or UK GDPR for EU and UK residents, and local laws in markets such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan).

### Writing a good interview guide

```text
Warm-up (2 min):     "Tell me a bit about your business and your role."
Past behavior (10):  "Tell me about the last time you [booked / bought / chose] a ..."
                     "What did you try first? What happened next?"
Pain points (8):     "What was the most frustrating part?" "What did you do about it?"
Decision (5):        "What almost stopped you?" "Who else was involved?"
Wrap-up (2):         "Is there anything I should have asked but didn't?"
```

### How to measure success

Research succeeds when it changes something measurable. For every design implication you ship, name the metric it should influence (for example, fewer pre-sale questions about fees, or higher completion of the pricing step) and check it a few weeks later.

### Summary

Capture users' goals, tasks, context, anxieties and knowledge; express needs as jobs to be done; start with proto-personas and validate them; use lightweight research sources; and translate insights into specific design implications.

scenes.narration: A quick word on interviews. Ask about past behavior, not the future. Tell me about the last time you booked a salon appointment beats would you use an app for that? People are poor at predicting their own behavior. Ask open questions, follow up with why, and tell me more. Avoid leading questions like don't you think this is easy? Record only with consent, pay people fairly for their time, and never turn an interview into a disguised sales pitch.
scenes.onScreen:
Interview essentials
• Past behavior, not predictions
• Open questions and follow-ups
• No leading questions
• Consent, fair pay, no sales pitch
scenes.visual: Layout: two speech bubbles compared. 0-9s: a weak question 'Would you use...?' appears with a cross; 9-18s: a strong question 'Tell me about the last time...' appears with a tick; 18-26s: a consent checkbox ticks; 26-35s: a fair-pay icon appears.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Designing for everyone. Personas built only from demographics, with no goals or worries. Asking people to predict what they'd do. Letting AI invent themes that no customer actually said. And the most common of all: doing research, then ignoring it. Research only matters if it changes something. So for every design implication you ship, name the metric it should move, like fewer questions about fees, and check it a few weeks later.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Designing for everyone
• Demographic-only personas
• Asking for predictions
• Unverified AI themes
• Research that changes nothing
scenes.visual: Layout: mistake cards on a pinboard. 0-8s: five cards pin up with red markers; 8-16s: each card is replaced by a green corrected version; 16-24s: a metric card appears: 'Fewer fee questions'; 24-32s: a check-back date appears on a calendar.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Capture goals, tasks, context, anxieties and knowledge for each key audience. Use jobs-to-be-done statements to decide what belongs on the page. Start with proto-personas and mark what's assumed. Mine the messages you already have, cluster them, and turn themes into design implications. Use AI for a first pass, verify every quote, and protect privacy. Try this now. Export twenty recent customer messages, reviews or support tickets. Anonymize them, cluster them into themes, and write three insight cards, each with one design implication and one metric to watch.
scenes.onScreen:
Recap and try this now
• Goals, tasks, context, anxieties, knowledge
• Jobs to be done
• Proto-personas: mark assumptions
• Cluster 20 messages; write 3 insight cards
scenes.visual: Layout: recap card with an insight card thumbnail. 0-10s: recap bullets animate in; 10-20s: three insight cards fan out; 20-29s: each shows a metric tag; 29-39s: closing text: 'Next: user flows and journeys'.

keyTakeaways: Capture goals, tasks, context, anxieties and knowledge for each key audience.
Jobs-to-be-done statements focus design on the progress users want to make.
Proto-personas are quick starting points — mark assumptions and validate them.
Interview about past behavior, avoid leading questions and turn insights into design implications.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which interview question is most useful?
options: 'Don't you think our design is easy?'
'Would you use an app like this?'
'Tell me about the last time you booked an appointment for your salon.'
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Questions about specific past behavior yield reliable insight; hypothetical and leading questions do not.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a proto-persona different from a research-based persona?
options: It's built quickly from team knowledge and assumptions, to be validated over time
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Proto-personas are quick, assumption-based profiles built from what the team already knows, then validated and updated as research accumulates; photos and completeness are not what defines them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Research shows users worry about hidden fees. What's the best design implication?
options: Show total costs clearly and early, including fees
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Addressing the anxiety directly with transparent pricing builds trust.

lessons.activity: Review 20 recent customer messages, reviews or support tickets. Cluster them into themes, write three insight statements and one design implication for each.

modules.title: Flows, structure and interface copy
modules.summary: Map user flows and journeys, organize navigation and content, and write clear microcopy for buttons, forms and errors.

lessons.title: User flows and journey maps
lessons.body:
### Seeing the whole path

Marketers often design single pages, but users experience **paths**: an ad, a landing page, a form, an email confirmation, a reminder, a purchase. Problems frequently hide between pages. User flows and journey maps make those paths visible.

### User flows

A **user flow** is a diagram of the steps a user takes to complete a task, including decisions and alternative paths.

Basic notation:

```
[Entry point] → (Page/screen) → {Decision?} → (Page) → [Goal]
                                   ↓ no
                               (Alternative path)
```

Example — webinar registration from Instagram:

```
[Instagram story ad] → (Landing page) → {Registered before?}
    ↓ no                                       ↓ yes
(Form: name + email) → (Thank-you page + calendar link) → [Registered]
    ↓ error
(Inline error message) → back to form
[Registered] → (Confirmation email) → (Reminder 1 day before) → (Reminder 1 hour before) → [Attends]
```

What to look for:

- **Number of steps** — can any be removed or combined?
- **Dead ends** — pages with no clear next step.
- **Error paths** — what happens when something goes wrong?
- **Channel switches** — moving from app to browser, social to website, email to WhatsApp — each switch risks drop-off.
- **Logged-in vs new users** — different paths.

### Happy path and edge cases

The **happy path** is the ideal route with no problems. Real users take many others:

- Payment declined.
- Email typed wrongly.
- Arriving from a shared link on a different device.
- Returning later to finish.
- Using a screen reader or keyboard only.
- Slow or interrupted connections.

Design at least the most common edge cases explicitly.

### Journey maps

A **customer journey map** zooms out further, capturing stages, actions, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the whole relationship.

| Stage | Aware | Consider | Sign up | Onboard | Use/Renew |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Actions | Sees reel | Visits site, reads reviews | Starts trial | Sets up account | Uses weekly |
| Touchpoints | Instagram | Website, Google reviews | Sign-up form | Emails, app | App, support |
| Thoughts | "Could this help me?" | "Is it worth the price?" | "Is this safe?" | "How do I start?" | "Is it still worth it?" |
| Feelings | Curious | Unsure | Anxious | Overwhelmed | Satisfied / frustrated |
| Opportunities | Clear promise | Transparent pricing, proof | Minimal form, trust signals | Guided setup | Tips, renewal reminders |

Journey maps help marketing, sales, product and support teams see their part of the same experience.

### Creating a flow: step by step

1. Choose one important task and entry point.
2. List every screen, message and decision.
3. Walk the flow yourself on mobile, taking screenshots.
4. Mark friction points: extra steps, unclear copy, slow loads, errors.
5. Add analytics data where available (drop-off at each step).
6. Propose a simplified flow.

### Worked example: a consultation booking flow

Original: Facebook ad → homepage → Services page → Contact page → long contact form → "We'll get back to you" → email back-and-forth to choose a time.

Problems: too many steps, the ad lands on the homepage (weak message match), no instant booking, uncertainty after submitting.

Redesign: ad → dedicated landing page matching the ad → embedded scheduler showing available times in the visitor's time zone → short form (name, email, one qualifying question) → confirmation page and calendar invite → reminder emails/SMS with consent.

### Common mistakes

- Designing screens in isolation.
- Ignoring error and edge-case paths.
- Forgetting post-conversion steps (confirmation, onboarding).
- Mapping the journey the company wishes existed rather than the real one.

### Measuring a flow

Once a flow is mapped, attach numbers to it. Most analytics tools can show how many people reach each step and where they leave. Even rough figures change priorities: a step that loses half of mobile visitors deserves attention before a cosmetic issue elsewhere. Record the baseline before you change anything, so you can compare results fairly afterwards and explain the improvement to your team or client.

### Hands-on: map a real flow with Mermaid and your analytics

You can draw flows on paper, in FigJam or Miro, or as text. Text diagrams are easy to version and share. Mermaid syntax renders in many tools (including GitHub, Notion and several documentation platforms, and there is a free live editor at mermaid.live). Here is the webinar flow from this lesson:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Instagram story ad] --> B(Landing page)
    B --> C{Registered before?}
    C -- No --> D(Form: name + email)
    C -- Yes --> H(You're already registered + calendar link)
    D -- Error --> E(Inline error message) --> D
    D -- Success --> F(Thank-you page + calendar link)
    F --> G(Confirmation email)
    G --> I(Reminder 1 day before)
    I --> J(Reminder 1 hour before)
    J --> K[Attends]
```

Now attach numbers. In GA4, an **Explore → Funnel exploration** lets you define each step as an event or page view and shows how many users reach each step (make sure the events exist and consent rules are respected before you rely on the numbers):

```text
Funnel steps (example event names — use your own)
Step 1  page_view        page_location contains /webinar
Step 2  form_start       (form interaction on the page)
Step 3  generate_lead    (form submitted successfully)
Step 4  webinar_join     (sent from your webinar platform, if integrated)
Breakdown: device category   Segment: session source = instagram
```

Write the step counts onto your diagram. The step with the largest relative drop is usually where to look first.

```text
FLOW FRICTION LOG
Step | What the user sees | Friction observed | Evidence (data/recording/test) | Fix idea | Effort (S/M/L)
```

### Edge-case checklist for any conversion flow

```text
[ ] Payment declined or bank verification step (3-D Secure) fails
[ ] Email typed wrongly — can the user correct it?
[ ] User returns later on another device (magic link, saved cart)
[ ] Link opened inside a social app's in-app browser
[ ] Keyboard-only or screen-reader user
[ ] Slow or interrupted connection mid-submit (double submissions?)
[ ] Right-to-left language version (Arabic, Urdu)
[ ] Consent declined for marketing messages — do reminders still work where lawful?
```

### How to measure success

A flow improvement should show up as a higher completion rate for the whole path (for example, ad click to confirmed booking), not just a better number on one page. Track the end-to-end rate before and after, by device and traffic source, and check post-conversion steps too: confirmed attendance, activation or repeat purchase.

### Summary

Use user flows to map task paths, including decisions and errors, and journey maps to see stages, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the relationship. Walk flows on mobile, mark friction, and simplify.

scenes.narration: Here's something marketers often miss. Nobody experiences your landing page on its own. They experience a path. An ad, a page, a form, a confirmation email, a reminder, maybe a WhatsApp message. And problems love to hide between the pages, where nobody on the team owns them. In this lecture, you'll learn to map user flows and customer journey maps, how to design for the edge cases real people hit, how to attach analytics numbers to every step, and how to simplify a flow so more people reach the finish line.
scenes.onScreen:
User flows and journey maps
• People experience paths, not pages
• Problems hide between pages
• Map, measure, simplify
scenes.visual: Layout: horizontal path of connected screens. 0-10s: an ad, a page, a form, an email and a reminder appear as linked tiles; 10-20s: red cracks appear in the gaps between tiles; 20-30s: a spotlight sweeps across the gaps; 30-40s: the title card fades in.

scenes.narration: Why does this matter? Because every extra step, every channel switch and every unclear moment leaks people. Think of a flow like a garden hose with small holes. Each hole on its own looks harmless. But by the end of the hose, only a trickle comes out. Most teams try to fix this by pushing more water in, meaning more ad spend. Mapping the flow shows you where the holes are, so you can patch them instead. That's usually far cheaper than buying more traffic.
scenes.onScreen:
Why it matters
• Every step leaks people
• The leaky hose analogy
• Patch holes before buying more traffic
scenes.visual: Layout: garden hose illustration. 0-9s: water flows into a hose from the left; 9-18s: small leaks spray from several holes; 18-28s: only a trickle exits on the right; 28-37s: patches cover the holes and the flow at the end strengthens.

scenes.narration: First, user flows. A user flow is a diagram of the steps someone takes to complete one task, including decisions and alternative paths. The notation is simple. Entry points and goals in square boxes. Pages or screens in rounded boxes. Decisions in diamonds, with arrows for yes and no. When you look at a flow, check five things. How many steps are there, and can any be removed or combined? Are there dead ends with no next step? What happens on error? Where does the user switch channels, like app to browser or email to WhatsApp? And do new and returning users take different paths?
scenes.onScreen:
User flows
• Boxes for entry, pages and goals
• Diamonds for decisions
• Check: steps, dead ends, errors
• Channel switches, new vs returning
scenes.visual: Layout: flow diagram drawing itself. 0-12s: an entry box and a page box connect with an arrow; 12-23s: a decision diamond splits into yes and no paths; 23-34s: an error loop appears in red; 34-46s: five check icons appear beside the diagram.

scenes.narration: Next, the happy path versus reality. The happy path is the ideal route where nothing goes wrong. Real people take many other routes. Their payment is declined. They mistype their email. They open your link inside Instagram, then try to finish on a laptop. They use a screen reader or only a keyboard. Their connection drops mid-submit. Here's the key idea. You don't need to design every possible edge case. But you must design the common ones deliberately, because those are where real customers quietly give up.
scenes.onScreen:
Happy path vs reality
• Payment declined
• Mistyped email
• Device switch mid-task
• Keyboard or screen reader • dropped connection
scenes.visual: Layout: a straight green path with branching red detours. 0-10s: a green line runs from start to goal; 10-19s: red branches split off: card declined, typo, device switch; 19-28s: each branch ends in a dead-end icon; 28-38s: the branches reconnect to the goal after fixes are added.

scenes.narration: Now zoom out. A customer journey map shows the whole relationship, not just one task. Columns are stages, like aware, consider, sign up, onboard and renew. Rows capture what people do, where they do it, what they think, how they feel, and your opportunities. For example, at the sign-up stage someone might think, is this safe? and feel anxious. The opportunity is a short form and clear trust signals. Journey maps are great for getting marketing, sales, product and support to see their part of the same experience.
scenes.onScreen:
Customer journey maps
• Stages: aware to renew
• Rows: actions, touchpoints, thoughts, feelings
• Opportunities per stage
• Aligns teams
scenes.visual: Layout: journey map grid filling in. 0-10s: five stage columns appear; 10-19s: rows for actions, touchpoints, thoughts and feelings fill in; 19-28s: an emotion line dips at 'Sign up'; 28-38s: an opportunity card appears under the dip.

scenes.narration: Worked example one, simple. A webinar from an Instagram story ad. The flow: ad, landing page, a two-field form, a thank-you page with a calendar link, a confirmation email, then reminders one day and one hour before. Walking it on a phone, we spot two problems. There's no error path, so a mistyped email just fails silently. And the calendar link opens a blank page inside Instagram's in-app browser. The fixes: inline error messages that say exactly what to correct, and a calendar option that works in in-app browsers, plus the link again in the confirmation email.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 1: webinar flow
• Ad → page → 2-field form → thank-you
• Silent failure on mistyped email
• Calendar link breaks in-app
• Inline errors + link in email
scenes.visual: Layout: Mermaid-style flow on screen. 0-10s: the flow diagram draws top to bottom; 10-21s: a red marker lands on the form's missing error path; 21-32s: a second marker lands on the calendar link; 32-42s: fixed nodes turn green.

scenes.narration: Worked example two, a business scenario with illustrative numbers. A consultancy in Riyadh runs Facebook ads for free strategy calls. The original flow: ad to homepage, then services page, contact page, a ten-field form, and a message saying we'll get back to you. Then days of email back and forth to find a time. Mapping it with analytics shows most mobile visitors never leave the homepage. The redesign: ad to a dedicated page that matches the ad, an embedded scheduler showing times in the visitor's time zone, a short form with one qualifying question, an instant confirmation and calendar invite, and reminders by email or text with consent.
scenes.onScreen:
Worked example 2: consultancy (illustrative)
• Six steps + email back-and-forth
• Most mobile visitors stop at homepage
• Dedicated page + embedded scheduler
• Instant confirmation and reminders
scenes.visual: Layout: before-and-after flow diagrams. 0-12s: the long original flow draws in gray, tagged Illustrative; 12-24s: a funnel overlay shows a big drop at the homepage; 24-35s: the flow collapses into a short new version; 35-47s: a calendar invite icon pops at the end.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. I pick one task: register for a webinar from Instagram. I write the flow as a text diagram in Mermaid syntax, which renders in many tools, so it's easy to share and update. Then I open GA4, go to Explore, and create a funnel exploration. Step one, page view on the webinar page. Step two, form start. Step three, generate lead. I break it down by device and filter to Instagram traffic. I write each step's numbers onto the diagram. The biggest relative drop is between form start and generate lead on mobile. That's where I'll look at recordings first.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me do it: flow + funnel
• Write the flow in Mermaid
• GA4 Explore → Funnel exploration
• Steps: page view, form start, lead
• Break down by device; find the biggest drop
scenes.visual: Layout: split screen of a text editor and an analytics funnel. 0-11s: Mermaid text types and renders into a diagram; 11-22s: a funnel exploration builds three steps; 22-34s: device breakdown bars appear; 34-45s: step counts copy onto the diagram and the biggest drop pulses.

scenes.narration: A few practical notes on that walkthrough. The funnel is only as good as your tracking. Make sure each event actually fires, and that your analytics respect consent rules, before you trust the numbers. Keep a friction log beside the diagram, with each step, what the user sees, the friction you observed, the evidence, a fix idea, and the effort. And use the edge-case checklist from the lesson. Card declined. Mistyped email. Device switch. In-app browser. Keyboard and screen-reader users. Slow connections. Right-to-left language versions. Five minutes with that list prevents weeks of silent losses.
scenes.onScreen:
Make the map trustworthy
• Verify events fire; respect consent
• Friction log beside the diagram
• Run the edge-case checklist
scenes.visual: Layout: checklist panel beside the flow diagram. 0-10s: a tick appears on 'events verified'; 10-20s: a friction log table fills two rows; 20-31s: the edge-case checklist scrolls with items ticking; 31-41s: a caption reads 'Five minutes, weeks saved'.

scenes.narration: Let's talk about the finish line, because many teams stop measuring too early. A webinar registration isn't the real goal. Attendance is. A trial sign-up isn't the goal. Activation is. So when you map a flow, include the steps after the conversion: the confirmation, the reminders, the first login, the first use. Then record a baseline for the whole path before you change anything. After the change, compare the same traffic sources over a similar period, split by device. If registrations rise but attendance falls, you haven't improved the flow. You've just moved the leak further down the hose.
scenes.onScreen:
Measure to the real finish line
• Registration → attendance
• Trial → activation
• Baseline the whole path
• Same sources, same period, by device
scenes.visual: Layout: extended funnel with post-conversion steps. 0-11s: a funnel ends at 'Registered'; 11-22s: three more steps extend it: confirmation, reminder, attended; 22-32s: a baseline line is drawn across all steps; 32-43s: a leak icon moves down the funnel when only the top improves.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Designing screens in isolation, one page at a time. Ignoring error paths, so failures are silent. Forgetting what happens after conversion, like confirmation, onboarding, and the reminder that gets people to actually show up. Mapping the journey the company wishes existed, not the real one. And measuring only one page instead of the whole path. The right success metric is end-to-end completion, like ad click to confirmed booking, split by device and source. If that number improves, the flow improved.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Screens designed in isolation
• No error paths
• Ignoring post-conversion steps
• Mapping the ideal, not the real
• Measuring one page, not the path
scenes.visual: Layout: mistake list beside an end-to-end metric. 0-9s: mistake cards appear with red icons; 9-18s: each card flips to its fix; 18-27s: an end-to-end metric bar from 'ad click' to 'confirmed booking' appears; 27-36s: the bar grows after fixes.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. People experience paths, not pages. User flows map the steps, decisions, errors and channel switches for one task. Journey maps capture stages, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the whole relationship. Design the common edge cases on purpose, attach real funnel numbers, and measure end-to-end completion. Try this now. Take one of your ads or posts and map the full flow to conversion, including at least two edge cases. Add numbers from your analytics if you have them, mark every friction point, and draw a simplified version with fewer steps.
scenes.onScreen:
Recap and try this now
• Paths, not pages
• Flows for tasks; journeys for relationships
• Design edge cases; add numbers
• Map one ad-to-conversion flow today
scenes.visual: Layout: recap card with a mini flow diagram. 0-10s: recap bullets animate in; 10-20s: a mini flow shrinks from seven steps to four; 20-30s: a completion rate badge increases; 30-40s: closing text: 'Next: information architecture'.

keyTakeaways: Users experience paths, not pages — map them.
User flows show steps, decisions, errors and channel switches for one task.
Journey maps capture stages, actions, thoughts, feelings and touchpoints across the relationship.
Design common edge cases, not just the happy path.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the 'happy path' in a user flow?
options: The ideal route through a task with no problems
A path for returning customers only
The path with the most steps
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It's the ideal route; real users also encounter edge cases that need design.

knowledgeCheck.question: A consultation flow requires email back-and-forth to choose a time. What is the most effective improvement?
options: Ask users to call during office hours only
Embed a scheduler showing available times so users book instantly
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An embedded scheduler lets people book instantly, removing email back-and-forth and the uncertainty of waiting; more fields or phone-only booking add friction.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which element belongs in a customer journey map but usually not in a simple user flow?
options: Users' thoughts and feelings at each stage
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Journey maps capture emotional and cognitive context across stages.

lessons.activity: Map the flow from one of your ads or social posts to conversion, including at least two edge cases. Mark every friction point and draw a simplified version.

lessons.title: Information architecture and navigation
lessons.body:
### Helping people find things

**Information architecture (IA)** is the structure and labeling of content so people can find what they need and understand where they are. Poor IA shows up as "I couldn't find your prices", high bounce rates, and lots of support questions that the website already answers somewhere.

### Core IA concepts

| Concept | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Organization | How content is grouped | By service, by audience, by task |
| Labeling | What groups and links are called | "Pricing" vs "Investment" |
| Navigation | How people move around | Header menu, footer, breadcrumbs, search |
| Search | Finding by query | Site search, filters |
| Hierarchy | Levels of content | Home → Services → Service detail |

### Labels in users' words

Labels are one of the biggest findability factors. Use words your users use (from interviews, search queries and support tickets), not internal jargon or clever branding.

| Weak label | Clearer label |
|---|---|
| Solutions | Services |
| Investment | Pricing |
| Our Journey | About us |
| Resources Hub | Guides / Blog |
| Connect | Contact |

Creative labels can be fine for brand personality in content, but navigation should be clear.

### Navigation patterns

- **Header navigation:** 4–7 top-level items is a common, manageable range for small business sites. Put the most important tasks first.
- **Primary call to action** in the header (e.g. "Book a call", "Start free trial").
- **Mobile navigation:** a menu icon with a clear label or recognizable icon; keep the key CTA visible outside the menu if possible.
- **Footer:** secondary links — policies, careers, social links, contact details.
- **Breadcrumbs:** for deeper sites (shops, knowledge bases).
- **Search:** essential for large content libraries and shops.

### Organizing content: card sorting

**Card sorting** is a simple research method to understand how users group content:

- **Open card sort:** users group topics and name the groups themselves — reveals mental models and labels.
- **Closed card sort:** users place topics into predefined categories — tests your structure.

Can be done with paper cards or online tools, with even a small number of participants.

**Tree testing** checks whether people can find items in a proposed menu structure (text-only), before any visual design.

### Sitemaps

A **sitemap** (for planning, not the XML file for search engines) shows every page and its hierarchy:

```
Home
├── Services
│   ├── Brand identity
│   ├── Social media content
│   └── Websites
├── Work (case studies)
├── Pricing
├── About
├── Blog
└── Contact / Book a call
```

For marketing sites, keep hierarchy shallow — key pages should be reachable within one or two taps.

### Landing pages and navigation

Dedicated campaign landing pages often **remove or reduce main navigation** to keep focus on one conversion goal. This can improve conversion but should still allow users control: keep the logo link or a minimal footer, and provide essential information (pricing, privacy policy, contact) so trust isn't harmed.

### Multilingual and RTL considerations

For sites serving English, Arabic and Urdu audiences:

- Provide an obvious language switcher (language names in their own script: "English", "العربية", "اردو").
- Mirror navigation for right-to-left languages.
- Keep equivalent structure across languages so users can switch without getting lost.

### Worked example: an agency website restructure

Problem: prospects couldn't find pricing or examples; menu had nine items with creative labels ("The Lab", "Our DNA", "Let's Talk Magic").

Process: reviewed site search and sales call questions; ran an open card sort with eight clients; tree-tested a new structure.

New IA: Services, Work, Pricing, About, Blog, plus a "Book a call" button. Case studies filterable by industry. Result tracked: more visits to pricing and case studies, and fewer "what do you charge?" emails (measured over the following quarter).

### Common mistakes

- Clever labels that hide meaning.
- Too many top-level menu items.
- Organizing by internal team structure instead of user tasks.
- Hiding essential information in footers or PDFs.

### Hands-on: test your navigation labels in an afternoon

**Step 1 — Collect your users' words.** Export the top site-search terms (GA4 can report the `view_search_results` event with the search term when enhanced measurement site search is enabled), plus the most common questions from sales calls and DMs. Write down the exact phrases.

**Step 2 — Draft two candidate structures.** Keep top-level items to a manageable number and use the words you collected.

**Step 3 — Run a quick tree test.** Dedicated tools exist (for example Optimal Workshop's Treejack, Maze and Lyssna offer tree testing), but a spreadsheet version works for a first pass with five to ten people:

```text
TREE TEST (text-only menu, no visual design)
Show participants this structure:
  Services > Brand identity | Social media content | Websites
  Work
  Pricing
  About
  Blog
  Contact

Tasks (don't reuse the menu words):
  T1  "You want to know roughly what a new logo would cost. Where would you click?"
  T2  "You'd like to see examples of work for restaurants. Where would you go?"
  T3  "You want to ask about a job opening. Where would you look?"

Record per task: first click | final answer | correct? (Y/N) | time | confidence (1-5)
Success target: at least 4 of 5 participants find each item on their first or second try.
```

**Step 4 — Fix the labels that fail**, and re-test just those tasks.

### Label audit template

```text
Current label | What users call it (evidence) | Proposed label | Tree-test success before/after
Investment    | "price", "cost", "packages"   | Pricing        | 2/6 -> 6/6
Our DNA       | "about", "team"               | About us       | 3/6 -> 5/6
```

### Navigation for AI-assisted and voice search

Clear, descriptive labels and a logical hierarchy also help search engines and AI answer engines understand what each page is about. Use descriptive page titles and headings that match the navigation label, add breadcrumbs on deeper sites, and keep important pages reachable through normal links rather than only through scripts or search boxes.

### How to measure success

Watch four signals after changing your IA: tree-test success rates, visits reaching key pages (pricing, case studies) from the homepage, site-search usage for items that are already in the menu (it should fall), and support or sales questions like "where can I find your prices?"

### Summary

Organize and label content in users' words, keep navigation focused and shallow, use card sorting and tree testing to validate structures, plan with a sitemap, and handle landing-page and multilingual navigation deliberately.

scenes.narration: Here's a real conversation that happens every week in small agencies. A prospect emails: what do you charge? And someone replies, it's on the website, under Investment. The prospect never found it. Not because they're lazy, but because nobody calls prices investment except the agency. That's an information architecture problem. In this lecture, you'll learn what information architecture is, how to label navigation in your users' words, how card sorting and tree testing work, and how to structure landing pages and multilingual sites so people find what they need in one or two taps.

scenes.narration: Information architecture, or IA, is the structure and labeling of content so people can find what they need and understand where they are. It has five parts. Organization: how content is grouped, by service, audience or task. Labeling: what groups and links are called. Navigation: how people move around, with header menus, footers and breadcrumbs. Search: finding things by typing. And hierarchy: the levels, like home, then services, then one service. Poor IA shows up as high bounce rates, lots of support questions the website already answers, and prospects who say they couldn't find your prices.
scenes.onScreen:
What IA is
• Organization • Labeling • Navigation
• Search • Hierarchy
• Symptoms: bounces, repeat questions

scenes.narration: Here's an analogy. Think about a supermarket. You walk in wanting rice. You don't know the store, but you find it in under a minute. Why? Clear signs above the aisles, in words you use, like rice and pasta, not carbohydrate solutions. Related things are grouped together. And the layout is similar to other supermarkets you've visited. A website works the same way. Clear signs are your navigation labels. Grouping is your organization. And familiarity is following conventions people already know, like pricing in the header and contact at the end.

• Grouped shelves = organization
• Familiar layout = conventions

scenes.narration: Labels are one of the biggest findability factors. Use the words your users use, from interviews, search queries and support tickets. Not internal jargon. Not clever branding. Solutions becomes Services. Investment becomes Pricing. Our Journey becomes About us. Resources Hub becomes Guides or Blog. Connect becomes Contact. Creative language can live in your content and headlines. But your navigation is a sign system, and signs must be instantly clear. For small business sites, four to seven top-level items is a common, manageable range, with the most important tasks first and one primary call to action in the header.

Labels in users' words
• Solutions → Services
• Investment → Pricing
• Our Journey → About us
• 4 to 7 top-level items + one CTA
scenes.visual: Layout: label swap animation on a header menu. 0-11s: a header shows five vague labels; 11-22s: each label flips to its clear version one by one; 22-32s: a 'Book a call' button appears on the right; 32-43s: a counter shows six top-level items.

scenes.narration: How do you know how users group things? Card sorting. In an open card sort, people group topics and name the groups themselves. That reveals their mental model and their words. In a closed card sort, they place topics into categories you've already defined, which tests your structure. Then there's tree testing. You show a text-only menu, no visual design, and give tasks like, you want to know what a new logo would cost, where would you click? If people can find it in the bare tree, your structure works. If not, no amount of visual polish will save it.

scenes.narration: Worked example one, simple. An agency website has nine menu items with creative labels: The Lab, Our DNA, Let's Talk Magic. Prospects can't find pricing or examples. The team reviews site search terms and sales call questions, and people keep saying price, cost, examples and portfolio. So they run an open card sort with eight clients, then tree-test a new structure. Services. Work. Pricing. About. Blog. Plus a Book a call button. And case studies filterable by industry. Over the next quarter, more visitors reach pricing and case studies, and the what do you charge emails drop.

scenes.narration: Worked example two, a business scenario with illustrative numbers. A furniture retailer in Dubai runs its site in English and Arabic. Arabic visitors browse fewer pages and use site search far more. A tree test with six Arabic-speaking customers reveals why. The Arabic menu was a literal translation, with categories organized differently from the English site, and the language switcher was a tiny flag icon. The fixes: an Arabic structure mirrored for right to left reading, category names chosen by Arabic-speaking customers, identical structure across both languages, and a switcher labeled in each language's own script.

scenes.narration: Watch me do it. First I collect words. In GA4, I check site search terms, and I pull the top questions from sales calls. Then I write two candidate structures in a spreadsheet. Next, a quick tree test with five people over video. I show only the text menu and give three tasks that don't reuse the menu words. For each task I record the first click, the final answer, and whether it was right. Task one, find logo pricing: two out of five succeed. That's a fail. I rename Investment to Pricing and re-test that one task. Five out of five.

scenes.narration: Two special cases. First, campaign landing pages. Many remove or reduce the main navigation to keep focus on one goal. That can help conversion, but keep essentials: the logo link, a minimal footer, and access to pricing, privacy and contact information so trust doesn't suffer. Second, multilingual sites. Provide an obvious language switcher with language names in their own script, mirror layouts for right to left languages, and keep the same structure across languages so people can switch without getting lost. And a bonus: clear labels and descriptive page titles also help search engines and AI answer engines understand your pages.

scenes.narration: A quick word on mobile navigation, because that's where most social traffic lands. The menu usually collapses behind an icon. Make sure that icon is recognizable, and consider adding the word menu next to it. Keep your primary call to action visible outside the menu, like a book a call button in the header, so people don't have to hunt for it. Put the most common tasks first inside the menu. Use breadcrumbs on deeper sites like shops and help centers. And add site search once you have a big content library. Then test it on a real phone, with your thumb, not a mouse.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Clever labels that hide meaning. Too many top-level items. Organizing by your internal team structure, like marketing department pages, instead of by user tasks. Hiding essential information in footers or PDFs. And skipping validation, because the structure seems obvious to the team. Remember, you're not your user. How do you measure success? Tree-test success rates. More homepage visitors reaching key pages like pricing and case studies. Less site search for things that are already in the menu. And fewer where can I find your prices questions.

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Information architecture is how content is organized and labeled so people can find it. Use your users' words for labels, keep navigation shallow and focused, validate structures with card sorts and tree tests, and handle landing pages and multilingual sites deliberately. Try this now. Draw a simple sitemap for your website or a client's. Rewrite any unclear navigation labels using words from real customer messages and search terms. Use labels in users' words, not internal jargon or clever branding.
Card sorting reveals mental models; tree testing validates a menu structure.
Keep navigation shallow and focused; plan landing-page and multilingual navigation deliberately.
